item.title: Utilities, Defense and Digitization are Driving Europe’s Capex Revival
item.content:encoded:
November 10, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

European companies are investing again. The capex-to-sales ratio is approaching a 10-year high, and European listed companies are expected to spend €77 billion more on capex in 2028 than in 2025, see charts below.

Utilities alone account for €31 billion, or around 40%, of the increase. Defense capex is expected to rise 36%, industrials excluding defense 24% and information technology 78%.

This comes after a long period of underinvestment. Across Europe, higher spending on energy, grids, defense, reshoring, infrastructure and digitalization is now lifting capital intensity.

The US capex cycle is dominated by AI. Europe's has a different mix: more of the increase is being driven by infrastructure, defense and power.

The bottom line is that capex is rebounding across Europe, and the industrial renaissance has gone global.

Written by Huw van Steenis

item.content:encoded:

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Through September 2026, the US labor market had kept unemployment below 5% for 61 straight months (since September 2021), putting it just three months shy of the record 64-month stretch set from 1965 to 1970, see chart below.

The bottom line is that the current expansion is on the verge of becoming the longest period of sustained labor market strength in modern US history, outlasting the late-1990s boom and every other run on record except one.

item.title: Is the CCC Stress Spreading to Single-B?
item.content:encoded:
November 05, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

When rates are higher for longer, stress in credit markets starts migrating from the bottom, beginning with the lowest-rated credit.

The ongoing widening between CCC and single-B shows that the weakest borrowers have run out of runway, and three things would need to happen for stress to migrate to single-B:

  1. Time. Single-B issuers have more cushion, but the cushion is finite. If rates stay at current levels, coverage ratios keep eroding as cheap debt reprices at maturity. Higher-for-longer is a slow leak for B, not a cliff, so the lag between CCC and B can be long.
  2. Access to capital. What keeps B stable is that the refinancing window is open. If it closes, through a risk-off shock or banks and private lenders pulling back, B issuers lose the ability to roll, and stress spreads quickly.
  3. Contagion through technicals. Rising CCC defaults can force CLO managers to hit CCC buckets, which constrains demand for B loans and pushes the two ratings together even without any change in B fundamentals.

The bottom line is that a single-B issuer typically has thin but positive free cash flow after interest. A CCC issuer often does not, so every quarter of elevated rates means more cash burn, a bigger PIK component and a growing reliance on refinancing windows or liability management exercises.

item.title: Iran: Severe Stress Now, More Risk If Conflict Returns
item.content:encoded:
November 04, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

Since the conflict began, Iran has seen inflation near 90%, a collapsing currency and oil exports falling to essentially zero.

Inflation is at 90%. Iranian consumer price inflation has surged to roughly 90% YoY, well above the previous peaks of around 50% seen in 2019-20 and 2022. Inflation had already been climbing before the conflict, but the pace of acceleration has increased sharply since it began.

The rial exchange rate is in free fall. On the open market, the rial has weakened to nearly 3 million per US dollar. The currency spent most of the last decade trending gradually lower, but the move has turned near-vertical since the conflict began. A weaker rial raises the cost of imports, which feeds directly into the inflation seen in the first chart.

Oil exports have collapsed. Crude exports, Iran’s main source of foreign currency, have fallen from roughly 1.8 million barrels per day to essentially zero. Iran has been through a similar episode before when exports dropped from over 2.5 million b/d in 2018 to very low levels through 2019-21 under sanctions, and only recovered gradually afterward. This time the fall is steeper and faster.

The bottom line is that the three charts are connected. Lost oil revenue means fewer dollars flowing into the country, which pushes the rial lower, which in turn drives import prices and inflation higher. Together, these charts point to severe stress on Iran’s economy, and this negative feedback loop continues for as long as exports remain shut in.

item.title: 10% Nominal GDP Growth Coming?
item.content:encoded:
November 03, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

Nominal GDP growth is currently solid at around 6%, while S&P 500 earnings growth has surged to nearly 40% YoY. A simple regression based on the historical relationship between the two suggests that the current pace of earnings growth is consistent with nominal GDP growth of 10%, see chart below.

The strong increase in corporate earnings and the resulting upside risk to GDP growth also point to upside risk to Friday’s employment report.

With strong earnings and upside risks to GDP growth and employment, the implication for investors is that interest rates will stay higher for longer, particularly when combined with the ongoing fiscal challenges.

item.title: How High Would the Fed Funds Rate Need to Rise to Bring Inflation Back to 2%?
item.content:encoded:
November 02, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

A macroeconomic model based on the historical relationship between interest rates, GDP and inflation suggests the Fed would need to raise the Fed funds rate by about 275 basis points, from roughly 4% today to 6.75% by the end of 2027, to bring CPI back to its 2% target. Inflation would not reach target until 2Q27, even with aggressive hikes.

The bottom line is that the Fed may be further from its inflation goal than the market currently expects.
